column2: L2 is per XCD (4 MiB each) and not shared; round-robin workgroup placement spreads data reuse across 8 L2s, so data shared by neighboring workgroups is fetched by multiple XCDs. Remap workgroup IDs so related tiles land on the same XCD.

column1: What is the Infinity Cache (MALL) on MI300X?
column2: A 256 MiB memory-attached last-level cache between the Infinity Fabric and HBM, peak ~17.2 TB/s. Working sets under 256 MiB may run faster than HBM peak; L2-to-fabric counters can then exceed 5.3 TB/s without being wrong.

column1: What is in an AQL kernel dispatch packet?
column2: 64-byte packet: header (type, barrier bit, acquire/release fence scopes), setup dims, workgroup sizes, grid sizes, private (scratch) and group (LDS) segment sizes, kernel_object (code descriptor address), kernarg address, completion signal.

column1: What happens between the doorbell write and the first wave?
column2: CP (MEC) sees the updated write index, fetches the AQL packet, honors barrier and acquire fence, reads the kernel descriptor, and the SPI splits the grid into workgroups, allocates VGPR/SGPR/LDS/wave slots on CUs, initializes system registers, launches waves. On completion: release fence, timestamps, decrement completion signal.

rocprofv3: ROCprofiler-SDK CLI for raw traces (HIP/HSA/kernel/memory) and named counters (--pmc). rocprof-compute: per-kernel analysis (Nsight Compute analog): multi-pass counter collection, roofline, speed-of-light panels. rocprof-sys: system timeline (Nsight Systems analog) with CPU sampling, MPI/OpenMP, GPU activity.
--hip-trace only traces HIP API calls; add --kernel-trace (or use --runtime-trace / --sys-trace). Also put -- before the application: rocprofv3 --hip-trace --kernel-trace -- ./app.

rocprof-compute profile -n NAME -- ./app (collects counters over multiple passes plus roofline benchmarks into workloads/NAME/ARCH), then rocprof-compute analyze -p workloads/NAME/ARCH (optionally -k to select kernels, -b for blocks) or the GUI/TUI to view speed-of-light, memory chart, and roofline.

column1: Why does rocprof-compute show a different kernel duration than a plain run?
column2: Counter collection serializes kernels (no overlap), adds packets and cache effects, uses multiple passes that each measure a slightly different run, and may change clocks. Use trace-only runs for timing and counter runs for ratios.

column1: Why do counter-collection tools serialize kernels?
column2: Hardware counters are device-wide (or per-SE/XCD) and not tagged per dispatch, so to attribute counts to one kernel the tool must ensure only that kernel runs between counter start and stop reads.

column1: Why do you need multiple passes to collect counters?
column2: Each hardware block has a few physical counter registers (e.g. 4 per block), so requesting more counters than fit requires replaying the workload (application replay) or the kernel (kernel replay) with different counter sets and merging results.

Application replay reruns the whole program per pass: simple, but costs N runs and needs determinism (hard for MPI). Kernel replay snapshots device memory and reruns one dispatch per pass in one run: identical inputs, but snapshot overhead and trouble with host-visible memory and atomics.

column1: GRBM_GUI_ACTIVE looks ~8x too large on MI300X. Why?
column2: It is accumulated per XCD and summed across the 8 XCDs. Divide by the XCD count (rocprof-compute's GRBM_GUI_ACTIVE_PER_XCD). Sanity check: GRBM_GUI_ACTIVE / XCDs / duration should give a plausible clock (1.5-2.4 GHz).

column1: How do you know a hardware counter is correct?
column2: Validate with microbenchmarks whose counts are known analytically (a copy kernel of N bytes, N FMAs), check invariants and cross-counter consistency (hits + misses = requests), compare against timing-derived values (bandwidth = bytes / time), and test across sizes and archs.

Host-trap (MI200+): driver-timed trap handler records the PC; has skid and little state. Stochastic (MI300+): hardware samples by cycle count with zero skid and records whether the instruction issued and the stall reason. Aggregate by PC and map to source lines.

column1: How does a GPU profiler intercept HIP calls without recompiling?
column2: ROCprofiler-SDK: runtimes register their API dispatch tables via rocprofiler-register at init; a tool exporting rocprofiler_configure (loaded via LD_PRELOAD or ROCP_TOOL_LIBRARIES) wraps the table entries. Generic alternative: LD_PRELOAD symbol interposition with dlsym(RTLD_NEXT).

Tells ROCr to dlopen listed libraries at hsa_init and call their OnLoad with the HSA API table, which they can patch. Older HSA-only hook used by the ROCm debug agent and legacy rocprof; ROCprofiler-SDK uses rocprofiler-register across HIP, HSA, ROCTx, RCCL.

column1: How does a profiler get per-kernel timing without modifying the app?
column2: It enables profiling on queues/dispatches so the command processor writes start/end timestamps into the completion signal (or uses barrier packets with timestamps), intercepting dispatch via API table wrapping, then converts GPU ticks to host time with a calibrated clock correlation.

column1: How does a profiler know a dispatch's kernel name?
column2: Intercept code object loading (hsa_executable APIs / HIP module registration) to map kernel_object addresses (kernel descriptors) to symbol names, then look up each AQL packet's kernel_object; demangle C++ names.

Report each unit's achieved throughput as a percent of its peak (VALU, MFMA, LDS, L1, L2, HBM). The highest-percentage unit is the likely bottleneck; if everything is low the kernel is latency- or launch-bound (look at occupancy, stalls, waitcnt).

column1: User says 30% VALU utilization means the kernel is bad. Response?
column2: Not necessarily: check whether it is memory-bound (high HBM/L2 bandwidth % of roof) or uses MFMA instead of VALU. Locate the kernel on the roofline; judge it against the relevant roof, not VALU.

column1: Diagnose a slow kernel with counters: steps?
column2: Get the duration and confirm the kernel matters (trace). Compute AI and place it on the roofline. Check SOL percentages per unit. Then drill down: occupancy and limiter (VGPR/LDS), cache hit rates, coalescing (bytes per request), LDS bank conflicts, divergence, stall reasons via PC sampling. Change one thing and re-measure.

Tail effects (too few workgroups, uneven last wave), short kernels dominated by launch and drain, workgroup-size granularity, LDS or barrier limits per workgroup, waves finishing at different times, or other concurrent kernels using CUs.

column1: Kernel launches 400 workgroups on a GPU that runs 304 concurrently. Efficiency loss?
column2: Two waves of workgroups: 304 then 96. Utilization = 400 / (2 x 304) = 66% if all workgroups take equal time (tail effect / wave quantization). Size grids to multiples of the concurrent capacity or use persistent kernels.

column1: Memory access fault: Page not present. How to debug?
column2: AMD_SERIALIZE_KERNEL=3 and AMD_LOG_LEVEL=3 to identify the kernel; ROCm debug agent (HSA_TOOLS_LIB=librocm-debug-agent.so.2) for wave state and PC; rocgdb with precise memory; compare the faulting address to the kernel's buffers; rebuild with GPU ASan (xnack+).

column1: Results differ slightly between runs. Bug?
column2: Usually not: floating-point atomics and reductions with nondeterministic order give different rounding. Check that differences are within expected tolerance (e.g. relative 1e-6 for FP32 sums), or use deterministic reductions if bitwise reproducibility is required.

column1: How do you test a GPU kernel for correctness?
column2: Compare against a reference implementation (CPU or simple GPU) in higher precision with dtype-appropriate tolerances, sweep sizes including non-multiples of tile sizes and edge cases (0, 1, huge), random seeds, adversarial values (NaN, inf, large magnitudes), and run under sanitizers.

hipify-perl/clang translate CUDA API names to HIP. Pitfalls: warp size 64 vs 32 (masks, shuffles, __activemask), hard-coded shared-memory sizes and occupancy assumptions, inline PTX, cooperative-group features, library differences (cuBLAS vs rocBLAS/hipBLAS).

column1: Ring allreduce time for S bytes on N GPUs?
column2: 2(N-1) steps, each sending S/N bytes: time ~ 2(N-1)/N x S/B + 2(N-1) x alpha. Bandwidth term approaches 2S/B independent of N (bandwidth-optimal), but latency grows linearly in N, so trees or hierarchical algorithms win for small messages.
algbw = S / time. busbw = algbw x 2(N-1)/N for allreduce, normalizing to per-link hardware bandwidth so you can compare against link peak independent of N.

column1: Why double binary tree in NCCL?
column2: A single tree uses only half the bandwidth (leaves only send). Two complementary trees where each rank is a leaf in one and interior in the other balance traffic, giving logarithmic latency with near-full bandwidth.

column1: DDP vs ZeRO-2 vs ZeRO-3/FSDP communication?
column2: DDP: allreduce gradients, ~2 Psi bytes per rank. ZeRO-2: reduce-scatter grads + all-gather params = same ~2 Psi. ZeRO-3/FSDP: all-gather params in forward and backward plus reduce-scatter grads = ~3 Psi, 1.5x DDP, in exchange for sharding all states.

column1: How does PyTorch DDP overlap communication with backward?
column2: Gradients are grouped into buckets (default 25 MB) in reverse order; autograd hooks fire when a bucket's gradients are all ready, launching an async allreduce while backward continues. Limits: the last bucket, unused parameters, and compute/comm kernels sharing CUs.

column1: 256-GPU job hangs in allreduce. Debug steps?
column2: Get stacks from all ranks (py-spy dump, gdb), enable NCCL_DEBUG=INFO / RCCL equivalent and TORCH_NCCL_* desync debug, find the rank that is missing or in a different collective (mismatched order or shapes, a rank that crashed or diverged in control flow), check network/xGMI errors. Use timeouts so it fails instead of hanging.

8 GPUs fully connected by xGMI (Infinity Fabric) links in a mesh rather than a switch, so each GPU has direct links to the other 7; RCCL uses multiple concurrent rings/direct algorithms to use all links, and per-link bandwidth is lower than a switch port.

NVIDIA MPS: multiple processes share one GPU's SMs concurrently via a server, with limited fault and memory isolation. MIG: hardware partitions with isolated memory and compute. AMD MI300X analog: CPX/NPS partition modes exposing XCDs as separate GPUs.

column1: Does a high-priority stream preempt a running kernel?
column2: Generally no: priority affects which pending workgroups the scheduler dispatches next, so new workgroups from the high-priority stream go first as CUs free up; running workgroups are not preempted (CU masking or partitioning is needed for hard isolation).

column1: What is Triton (the language) and why use it?
column2: A Python DSL for GPU kernels at the block level; the compiler handles thread mapping, coalescing, shared memory, and pipelining. Supports AMD (ROCm) and NVIDIA. Fast to write fused kernels (attention, layernorm) at near-hand-tuned performance; torch.compile emits Triton.

rocBLAS: classic BLAS on ROCm. hipBLASLt: flexible GEMM with epilogues and FP8, used by PyTorch for matmuls. Composable Kernel (CK): C++ template library of tile-based kernels for GEMM, attention, fused ops. MIOpen: convolutions/DNN primitives. RCCL: collectives.

Expected squared error = bias^2 + variance + irreducible noise. More data mainly reduces variance; more model capacity reduces bias but raises variance. Regularization trades a little bias for less variance.

column1: Why does L1 give sparse solutions and L2 not?
column2: The L1 ball has corners on the axes, so the loss contours typically touch it where some weights are exactly 0; its subgradient pushes small weights to 0 with constant force. L2's gradient shrinks proportionally to w, so weights get small but rarely exactly 0.

column1: Is weight decay the same as L2 regularization?
column2: Equivalent for plain SGD. Not for Adam: L2 added to the loss gets divided by the adaptive sqrt(v), so heavily updated weights are under-regularized. AdamW decouples decay (w -= lr * lambda * w) and is the standard.

column1: Train loss 0.01, val loss 2.3 and rising. Order of actions?
column2: Overfitting. First check for bugs and leakage between splits, then early stopping at the best val checkpoint, more data/augmentation, stronger regularization (weight decay, dropout), smaller model, and validate with cross-validation.

column1: Why does inverted dropout scale by 1/(1-p) in training?
column2: Keeps the expected activation the same between training (units dropped with probability p) and inference (no dropout), so no rescaling is needed at inference time.

column1: Gradient of softmax cross-entropy w.r.t. logits?
column2: dL/dz = softmax(z) - y (one-hot target). Clean, bounded gradient; compute with log-sum-exp (subtract the max) for numerical stability.
Training has many inputs (parameters) and one scalar output (loss). Reverse mode gets all partial derivatives in one backward pass (~2-3x forward cost); forward mode needs one pass per input.

column1: For Y = XW, what are dX and dW? Why is backward ~2x forward?
column2: dX = dY W^T, dW = X^T dY. Backward needs two matmuls of the same size as the one forward matmul, so ~2x FLOPs; training ~3x forward total, which gives the 6ND rule.

column1: Vanishing gradients and why residuals fix them?
column2: Repeated multiplication by Jacobians with norms < 1 shrinks gradients exponentially with depth (saturating sigmoids/tanh). Residual connections y = x + F(x) give an identity path, so the Jacobian is I + dF/dx and gradients flow directly.

ReLU zeros half the inputs, halving the variance of activations; doubling the weight variance keeps activation variance constant across layers. Xavier/Glorot uses 2/(fan_in + fan_out) for tanh-like activations.

LayerNorm normalizes across features per token, independent of batch size and sequence padding, identical at train and inference. BatchNorm depends on batch statistics, which are noisy for small/variable batches and sequences. RMSNorm drops mean-centering for speed.

m = b1 m + (1-b1) g; v = b2 v + (1-b2) g^2; m_hat = m/(1-b1^t); v_hat = v/(1-b2^t); w -= lr m_hat/(sqrt(v_hat)+eps). Bias correction fixes the zero initialization of m and v, which otherwise makes early steps too small.

column1: Memory to train a 7B model with AdamW mixed precision (no activations)?
column2: ~16 bytes per param: BF16 weights 2 + BF16 grads 2 + FP32 master weights 4 + Adam m 4 + v 4 = 16 B -> 112 GB. Needs sharding (ZeRO/FSDP) or larger GPUs; activations come on top.
A shorter averaging horizon for v (~20 steps vs ~1000) reacts faster to gradient-scale changes, reducing loss spikes and instability with large batches and long training.

column1: ROC-AUC 0.97 but useless for fraud. How?
column2: Extreme class imbalance: AUC measures ranking over all thresholds, including regions with many false positives that dwarf rare positives. Use precision-recall AUC and precision at the operating point; consider cost.
0.5: no better than random ranking. 0.3: worse than random, so the signal exists but is inverted (likely a label or sign bug); flipping the score gives 0.7.

column1: How do you check and fix calibration?
column2: Reliability diagram (predicted probability vs observed frequency), expected calibration error, Brier score. Fix on a held-out set with Platt scaling, isotonic regression, or temperature scaling for neural nets.
PPL = exp(mean negative log-likelihood per token). Not comparable across tokenizers because token counts differ; compare bits per byte/character or downstream task accuracy.

Never shuffle. Use rolling/expanding-window (walk-forward) backtests, train on the past and evaluate on the next period, avoid leakage from future features, and compare to naive and seasonal-naive baselines.

column1: Scaled dot-product attention formula and why divide by sqrt(d_k)?
column2: softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) V. If q and k entries have variance 1, q.k has variance d_k; dividing by sqrt(d_k) keeps logits at unit variance so softmax does not saturate and gradients do not vanish.
X: [B, T, D]. Q, K, V projections reshaped to [B, H, T, D/H]. Scores QK^T: [B, H, T, T]. Output after softmax x V: [B, H, T, D/H], concatenated to [B, T, D], then output projection D x D.

column1: How does RoPE encode relative position?
column2: Rotates pairs of dimensions of q and k by angles proportional to position; the dot product of rotated q_m and k_n depends only on (m - n). Applied to Q and K (which form scores), not V. Context extension uses scaling (NTK, YaRN).

MHA: separate K/V per head. MQA: one shared K/V head. GQA: groups of query heads share K/V (e.g. 64 Q heads, 8 KV heads), cutting KV cache and decode memory traffic 8x with little quality loss. LLaMA-2-70B and LLaMA-3 use GQA.
Attention: Q, K, V, O projections = 4 D^2. MLP with d_ff = 4D: 2 x 4 D^2 = 8 D^2. Total 12 D^2 per layer (ignoring biases, norms). Embeddings add V x D (vocab).
SwiGLU has three matrices (gate, up, down) instead of two; d_ff = 8D/3 keeps parameters at 3 x D x 8D/3 = 8 D^2, matching a 4D two-matrix MLP.

Pre-norm (x + F(LN(x))) keeps an unnormalized residual stream with an identity gradient path, so deep models train stably without long warmup. Post-norm can have better final quality but is harder to train deep.
Forward is ~2 FLOPs per parameter per token (one multiply-add), backward ~4, so training costs ~6 x N params x D tokens. Example: 70B x 15T tokens ~ 6.3e24 FLOPs.

Compute-optimal training uses ~20 tokens per parameter. With C = 6ND and D = 20N: C = 1e23 gives N ~ 29B, D ~ 580B tokens. In practice models are over-trained (LLaMA-3 8B on 15T tokens) because inference cost favors smaller models.

Model FLOPs Utilization = achieved model FLOPs/s (6ND / time) over hardware peak. Typical 35-55% for large training. Never 100%: communication, memory-bound ops (norms, softmax), pipeline bubbles, recomputation, and kernels below peak.

Process scores in blocks keeping running max m and sum l: m_new = max(m, max(x_blk)); l = l * exp(m - m_new) + sum exp(x_blk - m_new); output O = O * exp(m - m_new) + exp(x_blk - m_new) V_blk; finally O / l. Rescaling is correct because exp(x - m) terms are all expressed relative to the same final max.

column1: Why is FlashAttention faster despite more FLOPs?
column2: Attention is memory-bound in the naive form: the T x T score matrix is written to and read from HBM. FlashAttention tiles Q, K, V in on-chip memory with online softmax so scores never hit HBM, reducing HBM traffic from O(T^2) to O(T^2 d^2 / M); backward recomputes scores from saved per-row logsumexp.

FA2: fewer non-matmul FLOPs, parallelizes over sequence length too, better work split across warps (split Q not K). FA3 (Hopper): warp specialization with async TMA loads and wgmma, ping-pong between softmax and GEMM, FP8 support.

column1: Why is standard FlashAttention poor at decode?
column2: One query token per sequence gives little parallelism over the query dimension, so few workgroups. Flash-Decoding / split-K splits the KV sequence across workgroups and merges partial softmax results (using m and l).

column1: Why is decode memory-bound and prefill compute-bound?
column2: Decode processes 1 token per sequence: every weight is read for 2 FLOPs per weight per token, AI ~ batch size FLOP/B (for BF16, ~1 at batch 1) versus a ridge of ~250. Prefill processes thousands of tokens per weight read, AI in the hundreds or thousands.

2 (K and V) x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes x tokens. LLaMA-3-70B (80 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128, BF16): 2*80*8*128*2 = 327,680 B = 320 KiB per token. 32 users x 16K tokens ~ 172 GB, which with 140 GB of weights does not fit one 192 GB MI300X.

column1: Max batch-1 decode speed of a 70B BF16 model on MI300X?
column2: Weights 140 GB per token step / 5.3 TB/s = 26 ms -> ~38 tokens/s upper bound (realistically ~25-30). But 140 GB plus KV cache is tight on 192 GB; tensor parallelism across GPUs multiplies bandwidth.

column1: Throughput stops improving from batch 128 to 256. Why?
column2: Decode became compute-bound or KV-cache-bandwidth-bound (attention reads grow with batch x context while weight reads are amortized), or memory limits force preemption/swapping, or the scheduler and sampling become CPU-bound.

TTFT: time to first token (prefill + queueing). TPOT: mean time per output token after the first. ITL: inter-token latency distribution. Goodput: requests/s meeting SLOs. Chat: TTFT and ITL p99. Offline batch: throughput tokens/s.

Schedule at the iteration level: finished sequences leave and new ones join the batch every decode step, instead of waiting for the whole static batch to finish. Keeps the GPU full and cuts queueing; vLLM, SGLang, TGI use it.

Store the KV cache in fixed-size blocks (pages) with a per-sequence block table, like virtual memory, eliminating fragmentation from reserving max length, enabling prefix sharing (copy-on-write) and near-full memory use. vLLM's key idea.

Split long prompts into chunks interleaved with decode steps so a large prefill does not stall other users' token generation (bounds ITL), at the cost of slightly worse TTFT and extra KV reads per chunk.

A cheap draft model proposes k tokens; the target model verifies them in one forward pass. Accept token x with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)); on rejection sample from normalize(max(0, p - q)). Output distribution exactly matches the target; speedup depends on acceptance rate.

Run prefill and decode on separate GPU pools and transfer KV cache, when prefill interference hurts decode latency SLOs and the workload is large enough to justify KV transfer cost (fast interconnect). Lets each pool use different parallelism and batch sizes.

column1: Why does weight-only INT4 speed up decode but not prefill?
column2: Decode is bound by reading weights, so 4x fewer bytes is up to ~4x faster. Prefill is compute-bound and weights are dequantized to BF16 for the matmul, adding work, so no gain or even a slowdown.

GPTQ: layer-wise quantization using second-order (Hessian) information to compensate errors in remaining weights. AWQ: protects salient weight channels found from activation magnitudes via per-channel scaling, no backprop/reconstruction; simple and robust.

column1: Why is INT8 activation quantization hard and how does SmoothQuant help?
column2: LLM activations have a few outlier channels with huge magnitude, so a per-tensor scale wastes precision. SmoothQuant migrates scale from activations to weights with a per-channel factor (X diag(s)^-1)(diag(s) W), making both easy to quantize.

BF16: 8 exponent bits (FP32 range), 7 mantissa bits. FP16: 5 exponent, 10 mantissa; max 65504, needs loss scaling to avoid gradient underflow. BF16 replaced FP16 for training because its range removes overflow/underflow problems.

column1: BF16 machine epsilon and FP16 max?
column2: BF16 epsilon = 2^-7 ~ 0.0078 (7 stored mantissa bits). FP16 max = 65504, epsilon 2^-10 ~ 0.00098. FP32 epsilon 2^-23 ~ 1.2e-7.
E4M3: more precision, range up to 448 (OCP); used for weights and activations in the forward pass. E5M2: more range (up to 57344), less precision; used for gradients.

column1: OCP FP8 vs FNUZ FP8 on MI300X?
column2: MI300X (gfx942) natively implements FNUZ variants (no negative zero, single NaN encoding, exponent bias one higher so different max values: E4M3FNUZ max 240). OCP E4M3FN (max 448) is the standard used by NVIDIA and by MI350/MI355X. Converting checkpoints between them needs rescaling.

OCP MX: blocks of 32 elements share one 8-bit power-of-two scale (E8M0) with FP8/FP6/FP4 or INT8 elements. Small blocks handle outliers locally; power-of-two scales make scaling a cheap exponent add. Supported in hardware on MI355X and Blackwell.

column1: Dynamic loss scaling in FP16 training?
column2: Multiply the loss by S before backward so small gradients do not underflow; unscale before the optimizer. If any gradient is inf/NaN, skip the step and halve S; after N clean steps, double S.

column1: Why keep FP32 master weights with BF16 compute?
column2: Updates lr x grad are often smaller than BF16's precision relative to the weight (epsilon 2^-7), so they would round to zero; accumulating updates in FP32 preserves them.

column1: Why accumulate GEMMs in FP32 even with FP8 inputs?
column2: A dot product sums thousands of products; low-precision accumulation loses small addends (swamping) and overflows. Matrix cores multiply in low precision but accumulate in FP32.

column1: BF16 training is non-reproducible run to run on one machine. Broken?
column2: Usually not: atomic-based reductions, nondeterministic kernel selection (autotuning), and different split-K choices change summation order. For reproducibility set seeds, torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True), fixed algorithms, accepting slowdown.

column1: Data vs tensor vs pipeline vs sequence vs expert parallelism?
column2: Data: replicate model, split batch, allreduce grads. Tensor: split matmuls within a layer across GPUs (needs fast intra-node links). Pipeline: split layers into stages with micro-batches (bubbles). Sequence/context: split the sequence (ring attention). Expert: place MoE experts on different GPUs with all-to-all.
With p stages and m micro-batches (GPipe/1F1B), bubble ~ (p - 1) / (m + p - 1). Use m >> p (e.g. m = 4p) or interleaved schedules to shrink it.
Store only some activations (e.g. layer inputs) and recompute the rest in backward: cuts activation memory from O(L) to about O(sqrt(L)) or per-layer, at ~33% more compute (one extra forward).

~47B total parameters (experts share attention), ~13B active per token (top-2 of 8 experts). Compute per token is like a 13B model, but memory and serving must hold all 47B, and all-to-all routing adds communication.

Auxiliary loss encouraging uniform token distribution across experts (product of fraction routed and mean router probability). Without it routing collapses to a few experts, others are untrained, and capacity limits drop tokens.

Eager: runs ops one at a time, flexible and debuggable, launch and memory traffic overheads. torch.compile: TorchDynamo captures graphs from bytecode, AOTAutograd traces backward, Inductor fuses ops and generates Triton kernels; graph breaks fall back to eager.

column1: Why is torch.cuda/HIP timing with time.time() wrong?
column2: Kernel launches are async; time.time() measures launch time. Call torch.cuda.synchronize() before reading the clock or use CUDA/HIP events; warm up first to exclude compilation and allocator effects.

column1: PyTorch caching allocator and OOM fragmentation?
column2: PyTorch keeps freed GPU blocks in a cache to avoid hipMalloc/cudaMalloc costs; memory_reserved > memory_allocated. Fragmentation can OOM despite free memory; use expandable_segments in PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF (PYTORCH_HIP_ALLOC_CONF on ROCm), smaller fixed shapes, empty_cache only for debugging.

column1: Profile a slow PyTorch training step on MI300X end to end?
column2: torch.profiler (or rocprof-sys) to see CPU/GPU timeline: data loading stalls, launch-bound gaps, synchronizations (.item(), prints), communication overlap. Then rank top kernels by time, and use rocprof-compute on the hot kernels; check MFU vs expectations.

Training: throughput, MFU, scaling efficiency, fault tolerance via checkpointing. Inference: latency SLOs (TTFT, ITL), cost per token, memory for KV cache, batching policies, model loading and autoscaling.

Chunk documents, embed chunks, store in a vector index (HNSW/IVF), embed query, retrieve top-k (often hybrid with BM25), optionally rerank with a cross-encoder, assemble the prompt, generate, cite sources; evaluate retrieval recall and answer faithfulness.

column1: HNSW vs IVF-PQ for vector search?
column2: HNSW: graph-based, high recall and low latency, memory heavy, slow builds. IVF-PQ: cluster then search a few clusters with compressed (product-quantized) vectors; much less memory, lower recall; good for billions of vectors.

1) Clarify functional and non-functional requirements (scale, latency, consistency). 2) Back-of-envelope estimates (QPS, storage, bandwidth). 3) API and data model. 4) High-level diagram. 5) Deep dive on 1-2 hard components. 6) Bottlenecks, failure modes, trade-offs, monitoring.
Vertical: bigger machine; simple, limited and a single point of failure. Horizontal: more machines; needs stateless services, partitioning, load balancing, and handling partial failures.

L4 routes by IP/port (fast, protocol-agnostic, TLS passthrough). L7 parses HTTP: routing by path/header, TLS termination, retries, rate limits, sticky sessions, at higher CPU cost. Algorithms: round robin, least connections, consistent hashing, power of two choices.

column1: Cache strategies: cache-aside vs write-through vs write-back?
column2: Cache-aside: app reads cache, on miss loads DB and populates; writes go to DB then invalidate. Write-through: write cache and DB synchronously (consistent, slower writes). Write-back: write cache, flush later (fast, risk of loss).
When a hot key expires, many requests hit the DB at once. Fixes: request coalescing (single-flight lock per key), probabilistic early expiration, stale-while-revalidate, jittered TTLs.

Race: reader misses, reads old DB value; writer updates DB and deletes cache; reader then writes the stale value into cache. Mitigate with short TTLs, versioned keys, delete-after-delay (double delete), or CDC-driven invalidation.

SQL: relational data, joins, transactions, strong consistency, flexible queries. NoSQL (key-value, wide-column, document): massive scale-out writes, simple access patterns known upfront, flexible schemas, tunable consistency. Decide from access patterns.

Range sharding (good for scans, hot spots on sequential keys), hash sharding (even load, no range queries), directory/lookup-based. Hot keys: add salt/suffix, split the shard, cache. Resharding: consistent hashing or many virtual shards mapped to nodes.

Async replicas serve stale reads. Guarantees to add: read-your-writes (read own data from the leader or wait for an LSN), monotonic reads (stick a user to one replica), consistent prefix. Failover may lose acknowledged writes unless semi-sync.

Queue (RabbitMQ, SQS): messages deleted when acked, per-message routing, competing consumers. Log (Kafka): append-only partitioned log retained for time; consumers track offsets, can replay; ordering per partition; high throughput.

Order is guaranteed only within a partition. Messages with the same key go to the same partition. Max consumer parallelism in a group = number of partitions. Exactly-once with idempotent producers plus transactions.

Token bucket (allows bursts up to bucket size, refills at rate r), leaky bucket (smooths output), fixed window (boundary bursts), sliding window log (exact, memory heavy), sliding window counter (approximation). Distributed: Redis with atomic Lua/INCR, per-node local limits.

column1: Design a URL shortener: key points?
column2: Write ~100s/s, reads 100x more. ID generation: base62 of a counter (range allocation per server) or hash with collision check; 7 base62 chars = 3.5e12 IDs. KV store id -> URL, cache hot entries, 301 vs 302 (302 keeps analytics), expiry, abuse prevention.

Snowflake: 41-bit ms timestamp + 10-bit machine id + 12-bit sequence = 4096 IDs/ms per machine, roughly time-sorted, no coordination (watch clock skew). Alternatives: UUIDv4 (random, poor index locality), UUIDv7 (time-ordered), DB ticket servers.

column1: Design a news feed: fan-out on write vs read?
column2: Fan-out on write: push post IDs into followers' feed caches; fast reads, expensive for celebrities. Fan-out on read: merge followees' posts at read time; cheap writes, slow reads. Hybrid: push for normal users, pull for celebrities.

column1: Design a distributed key-value store (Dynamo style)?
column2: Consistent hashing with vnodes, replication factor N with quorum R/W, hinted handoff for temporary failures, Merkle-tree anti-entropy, vector clocks or LWW for conflicts, gossip membership, LSM storage engine.

column1: Design a GPU telemetry/profiling data pipeline?
column2: Agents on nodes collect counters/traces (sampled, batched, compressed), push to a durable log (Kafka) keyed by job/node, stream processors aggregate into time-series DB (downsampled rollups), raw traces to object storage with metadata index, query API and dashboards, alerting; control overhead and cardinality.

Client sends a unique key with a mutating request; the server stores key -> result and returns the stored result on retries. Makes retries safe (payments). Store with TTL and in the same transaction as the side effect.

After failures exceed a threshold, the breaker opens and calls fail fast; after a timeout it goes half-open and lets trial requests through; success closes it. Prevents cascading failures and gives a struggling dependency time to recover.
Only for idempotent operations or with idempotency keys; exponential backoff with jitter; retry budgets/caps to avoid retry storms; deadlines propagated across calls; do not retry at every layer.

When a consumer cannot keep up, signal producers to slow down (bounded queues that block or reject, TCP windows, reactive streams, 429/503 with Retry-After) rather than buffering unboundedly and running out of memory.

column1: Observability: metrics vs logs vs traces?
column2: Metrics: cheap aggregated numbers over time (RED: rate, errors, duration; USE: utilization, saturation, errors) for alerting. Logs: detailed events for debugging. Traces: per-request spans across services for latency attribution (OpenTelemetry).

SLI: measured indicator (p99 latency, success ratio). SLO: target for an SLI (99.9% of requests < 300 ms over 30 days). SLA: contractual promise with penalties. Error budget = 1 - SLO (43 minutes per month at 99.9%); spend it on releases.

column1: Availability nines in downtime per year?
column2: 99% ~ 3.65 days; 99.9% ~ 8.8 hours; 99.99% ~ 53 minutes; 99.999% ~ 5.3 minutes. Serial dependencies multiply availabilities (two 99.9% services ~ 99.8%).

Edge caches serve static and cacheable dynamic content near users, cutting latency and origin load. Control with Cache-Control/TTL, cache keys (URL + selected headers), versioned asset URLs for invalidation, origin shielding.

Metadata service (bucket/key -> chunk locations) separate from data nodes; files split into chunks replicated (3x) or erasure-coded (e.g. 6+3 for ~1.5x overhead); checksums, background repair, multipart upload.
Trie or prefix index of top-k completions per prefix precomputed offline from query logs, served from memory/cache, updated periodically; debounce client requests; shard by prefix.

Single responsibility, Open/closed (extend without modifying), Liskov substitution (subtypes honor base contracts), Interface segregation (small focused interfaces), Dependency inversion (depend on abstractions; inject dependencies).
Prefer composition: has-a relationships assembled from small parts, swappable at runtime, avoids fragile base classes. Use inheritance for true is-a substitutable relationships and interfaces.

Encapsulate interchangeable algorithms behind an interface and inject the one to use (sorting comparator, pricing rules, retry policy). In C++ often a template parameter or std::function; in Python a plain function.

Subjects notify registered observers on change (event listeners, signals/slots). Pitfalls: dangling observers (use weak_ptr or unsubscribe in destructors), notification order, re-entrancy, thread safety, memory leaks from never-removed listeners.

column1: Factory method vs abstract factory vs builder?
column2: Factory method: a function/virtual chooses which concrete class to create. Abstract factory: creates families of related objects (GPU backend: HIP vs CUDA objects). Builder: constructs complex objects step by step with optional parts and validation.

column1: Singleton: why controversial and how to do it in C++?
column2: Global state hides dependencies, complicates testing and init order. If needed: Meyers singleton (static local in a function), thread-safe since C++11. Prefer dependency injection.

column1: Adapter vs decorator vs proxy vs facade?
column2: Adapter: converts one interface to another. Decorator: same interface, adds behavior (logging, caching), stackable. Proxy: same interface, controls access (lazy load, remote, permission). Facade: simplified interface to a subsystem.
Encapsulate a request as an object with execute (and undo): undo/redo stacks, job queues, macro recording, transactional operations, GPU command buffers conceptually.

column1: Visitor pattern and its C++17 alternative?
column2: Double dispatch to add operations over a fixed class hierarchy without modifying it (AST passes). Downside: adding a new element type touches all visitors. Alternative: std::variant plus std::visit.
Represent each state as an object/class handling events and transitioning; avoids giant switch statements (vending machine, TCP connection, elevator). Simple cases: an enum plus transition table.
Template method: base class fixes the algorithm skeleton and subclasses override steps (inheritance). Strategy: inject the varying step as an object (composition), changeable at runtime.

Hide implementation in a pointer to an incomplete type in the header: stable ABI, faster builds (fewer header deps), hides private members. Cost: an indirection and heap allocation; define the destructor in the .cpp for unique_ptr to an incomplete type.

Clarify requirements and scope, identify entities and relationships, define classes and interfaces, key methods and state, concurrency concerns, extensibility (new vehicle types/pricing via strategy), then code core classes and walk a use case.

column1: Design a thread-safe bounded blocking queue?
column2: Mutex, two condition variables (not_full, not_empty), a deque with capacity. push waits on not_full with a predicate, pushes, notifies not_empty; pop symmetric. Add close() for shutdown that wakes all waiters.

Fixed worker threads loop popping tasks from a blocking queue; submit wraps callables in packaged_task and returns futures; shutdown sets a flag, notifies all, joins. Handle exceptions in tasks, avoid deadlock when tasks wait on other tasks (work stealing or larger pools).
Classes receive collaborators (constructor parameters/interfaces) instead of constructing them, enabling mocks in tests, configuration swaps, and clear dependency graphs.

column1: Plugin architecture in C++ for a profiler (new GPU arch support)?
column2: Stable C ABI or abstract interfaces loaded via dlopen + a factory symbol, version-checked; per-arch configs/data files (counter definitions, metric formulas) instead of code where possible; registry keyed by gfx target; tests per arch with recorded data.
Merge preserves history with a merge commit (non-destructive). Rebase replays your commits onto a new base for linear history but rewrites commit IDs; never rebase commits others have pulled.
All move HEAD (and the branch). --soft keeps index and working tree (changes staged). --mixed (default) resets the index, keeps working tree changes. --hard discards index and working-tree changes.
revert creates a new commit undoing a previous one: safe on shared branches. reset moves the branch pointer, rewriting history: only for local/unpublished commits.

column1: Recover a lost commit after a bad reset?
column2: git reflog shows where HEAD has been; git reset --hard HEAD@{n} or git branch rescue <sha>. Unreachable commits survive until gc (default reflog expiry 90 days, 30 for unreachable).
Binary search for the commit that introduced a bug: git bisect start, bad, good <sha>, then test each checkout; git bisect run ./test.sh automates it. log2(N) steps (1000 commits ~ 10 tests).

Content-addressed blobs (file contents), trees (directories), commits (tree + parents + metadata), annotated tags. Branches are refs (files containing a commit hash); HEAD points to a ref or commit (detached).
fetch downloads remote commits and updates remote-tracking refs without touching your branch. pull = fetch + merge (or rebase with pull.rebase=true).
Squash/fixup, reorder, reword, drop commits before publishing (git rebase -i base). Use git commit --fixup and --autosquash. Force-push with --force-with-lease to avoid clobbering others' work.
Applies the changes of specific commits onto the current branch as new commits (backporting fixes to release branches); use -x to record the source commit.

Inspect conflict markers (or a mergetool), understand both sides (git log --merge, git diff), edit, git add, continue (merge --continue / rebase --continue). Enable rerere to reuse resolutions. Run tests before committing.
stash saves uncommitted changes onto a stack (git stash push -m, pop, apply). git worktree add path branch checks out another branch in a separate directory sharing the same repo, no stashing needed.

column1: Find which commit changed a line or removed a string?
column2: git blame -L for line authorship (-w ignore whitespace, -C detect moves). git log -S 'string' (pickaxe) finds commits that added/removed it; -G regex for diffs matching.

column1: Linux: find which process listens on port 8080?
column2: ss -ltnp 'sport = :8080' (or lsof -i :8080). ss replaces netstat.

column1: Linux: process is slow; first commands?
column2: top/htop (CPU, state), pidstat 1, vmstat 1 (run queue, swap, iowait), iostat -x 1 (disk util/await), free -m, dmesg -T (OOM, hardware errors), strace -c -p PID (syscalls), perf top -p PID.

column1: Disk full but du shows less usage than df. Why?
column2: A deleted file is still held open by a process (space not freed until close). Find with lsof +L1 (or lsof | grep deleted) and restart/truncate via /proc/PID/fd/N. Also check inode exhaustion with df -i.
strace: system calls via ptrace (high overhead). ltrace: library calls. perf: sampling CPU profiler and hardware counters with low overhead; perf trace is a lower-overhead strace alternative.

column1: grep, sed, awk one-liners to know?
column2: grep -rn 'pat' dir; grep -v exclude; sed -i 's/old/new/g' file; awk '{sum += $3} END {print sum}'; awk -F, '$2 > 10 {print $1}' f.csv; sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head for top-N counts.

column1: Shell pipelines: exit status and safety flags?
column2: A pipeline's status is the last command's unless set -o pipefail. Use set -euo pipefail in scripts, quote variables ("$var"), and prefer $(...) over backticks.
Octal rwx bits for user/group/other: 755 = rwxr-xr-x (executables, dirs), 644 = rw-r--r-- (files). Directories need x to traverse. setuid (4xxx) runs as the file owner.

column1: Signals: SIGTERM vs SIGKILL vs SIGINT vs SIGHUP?
column2: SIGTERM (15): polite request, can be handled. SIGKILL (9): cannot be caught or ignored. SIGINT (2): Ctrl-C. SIGHUP (1): terminal hung up, often used to reload config. Containers send SIGTERM then SIGKILL after a grace period.

Namespaces isolate what a process sees (pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user, cgroup). cgroups limit and account resources (CPU, memory, I/O, pids). Containers are processes combining both plus a root filesystem (overlayfs).

Containers share the host kernel: fast startup, low overhead, weaker isolation. VMs run a full guest kernel on a hypervisor: strong isolation, more overhead. GPU access in containers needs device nodes (/dev/kfd, /dev/dri on AMD) and matching user-space drivers.

column1: Run a ROCm container with GPU access?
column2: docker run --device=/dev/kfd --device=/dev/dri --group-add video --security-opt seccomp=unconfined -it rocm/dev-ubuntu-22.04 (or a rocm/pytorch image). The host needs the amdgpu kernel driver; user-space ROCm lives in the image.

Order from least to most frequently changing (install deps before copying source), combine apt-get update and install in one RUN with cleanup, use .dockerignore, multi-stage builds to keep runtime images small, pin base image versions/digests.

ENTRYPOINT sets the executable; CMD provides default arguments (or the default command if no ENTRYPOINT). Use exec form (JSON array) so the process is PID 1 and receives signals; add an init (tini, --init) to reap zombies.

column1: CI pipeline essentials for a C++/GPU project?
column2: Build matrix (compilers, ROCm versions, Release/Debug), ccache, unit tests on CPU runners, GPU tests on self-hosted GPU runners with labels, sanitizer and clang-tidy jobs, artifacts and test reports, caching, required checks before merge.
Reproduce with repeated runs (--gtest_repeat, pytest-repeat), find root cause (timing, ordering, shared state, randomness, resource limits), quarantine with tracking, never just add retries silently.

break file:line, run, bt (backtrace), frame N, info locals, print expr, watch var (hardware watchpoint), thread apply all bt (for hangs), catch throw, core files: gdb ./app core. Build with -g and ideally -O0 or -Og.

column1: Debug a hang in a multithreaded process?
column2: Attach gdb -p PID and thread apply all bt, or eu-stack/py-spy dump; look for threads blocked on mutexes/condition variables and lock ordering cycles; check futex waits with strace; for GPU hangs check kernels in flight (rocgdb, debug agent).
ulimit -c unlimited, check /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern (often systemd-coredump: coredumpctl list / coredumpctl gdb). Containers need the pattern set on the host.

Valgrind memcheck: dynamic binary instrumentation, no recompile, 20-50x slowdown, also cachegrind/callgrind/massif. ASan: compile-time instrumentation, ~2x slowdown, catches stack and global overflows Valgrind misses; needs rebuild.

perf record -g (or --call-graph dwarf for code without frame pointers) -p PID -- sleep 10; perf report; for flame graphs: perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl | flamegraph.pl. Width = time on CPU; look for wide plateaus.
On-CPU profilers miss time spent blocked (locks, I/O, sleeps). Use off-CPU flame graphs (bpftrace/BCC offcputime, perf sched) to see where threads wait; combine with wall-clock profilers.

ROCm's gdb for host and GPU code: break in kernels, info agents/queues/dispatches, switch between waves (info threads lists waves), lane selection, and set amdgpu precise-memory on to stop at the faulting instruction.

column1: CMake: target_link_libraries PUBLIC vs PRIVATE vs INTERFACE?
column2: PRIVATE: used only to build this target. INTERFACE: only consumers need it (header-only). PUBLIC: both. Usage requirements (include dirs, definitions, flags) propagate transitively through PUBLIC/INTERFACE.

column1: Why modern target-based CMake over global variables?
column2: target_* commands scope flags, include dirs, and deps to targets and propagate usage requirements, avoiding leaks of include_directories/add_definitions to unrelated targets and making packages exportable.

Module mode uses FindXxx.cmake (shipped by CMake or you) that search for files. Config mode uses XxxConfig.cmake installed by the package itself, exporting imported targets (hip::host, roc::rocblas). Prefer config mode; set CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH (e.g. /opt/rocm).

Evaluated at generate time: $<CONFIG:Debug>, $<BUILD_INTERFACE:...>/$<INSTALL_INTERFACE:...> for include paths, $<TARGET_FILE:tgt>, $<$<CXX_COMPILER_ID:GNU>:-Wall>. Needed because config is unknown at configure time for multi-config generators.

project(x LANGUAGES CXX HIP) or enable_language(HIP), set CMAKE_HIP_ARCHITECTURES (e.g. gfx942;gfx950), mark .hip sources (or set_source_files_properties LANGUAGE HIP), find_package(hip) and link hip::device or hip::host as needed.

CMakePresets.json defines configure/build/test presets (generator, cache vars, binary dir) shared in the repo; CMakeUserPresets.json for local ones. cmake --preset dev, cmake --build --preset dev, ctest --preset dev.
ctest --output-on-failure, -R regex / -E exclude, -j N parallel, -L label, --rerun-failed, --repeat until-fail:N for flakiness, --test-dir build.

find_package: use an installed dependency. FetchContent: download at configure time and add_subdirectory it (part of your build). ExternalProject: build at build time as a separate project (isolated, harder to consume targets). FetchContent can try find_package first (FIND_PACKAGE_ARGS).

Situation (brief context), Task (your responsibility), Action (what you specifically did, the bulk, using I), Result (quantified outcome plus what you learned). Aim for ~2-3 minutes; keep S+T under ~20%.

column1: CARL format and when to prefer it?
column2: Context, Action, Result, Learning. Folds Situation and Task together and makes the lesson explicit; good for failure and growth stories and for compact answers.

Ownership, scope and impact, handling ambiguity and conflict, collaboration and influence, learning from failure, communication clarity, and level-appropriate judgment, backed by specific evidence of what you did.

column1: How many stories should a story bank have?
column2: About 8-12 strong stories, each tagged to multiple themes (conflict, failure, leadership, ambiguity, impact, mentoring, tight deadline, customer focus), so you can cover a full loop without repeating.

column1: Tell me about a time you failed: how to answer?
column2: Pick a real failure with meaningful stakes that you owned (not a disguised strength), explain your decision and what went wrong, what you did to recover, the concrete change you made afterwards, and evidence the lesson stuck.

Do: show you understood the other side's goals, used data or experiments to resolve, disagreed and committed, kept the relationship. Don't: blame, make the other person a villain, or win by escalation alone.

column1: What if my result is not quantifiable?
column2: Use proxies: time saved, adoption (teams/users), bugs avoided, decisions enabled, latency or turnaround reduction, qualitative feedback from customers or leads; state scale and before/after.

column1: I vs we in behavioral answers?
column2: Use I for your actions and decisions; use we for team outcomes. Interviewers must score your contribution; too much we hides it and is a common reason for down-leveling.
60-90 seconds: present role and scope (GPU profiling tools at AMD), one or two signature achievements with numbers, the through-line of your skills, and why this role now. Tailor emphasis per round.

column1: How to talk about unreleased hardware or confidential work?
column2: Describe the problem class, your approach, and relative results without product names, specs, or customer names; say I can't share specifics but here's the shape of it. Interviewers respect boundaries.

column1: Amazon Leadership Principles to prepare first?
column2: There are 16; prioritize Customer Obsession, Ownership, Dive Deep, Deliver Results, Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit, Earn Trust, Invent and Simplify, Bias for Action. Map each story to 2-3 LPs.

Ask about the team's biggest technical challenge this year, how success is measured in the first 6 months, how decisions are made on roadmap and design, on-call and release process, and what the interviewer enjoys or finds hard.

column1: How to explain GPU counter analysis to a non-GPU interviewer?
column2: Start with the user problem (why is my kernel slow), an analogy (a factory where you measure each machine's utilization), the key insight, then the outcome. Offer to go deeper rather than leading with jargon.

Recruiter screen, technical phone screen (coding), onsite/virtual loop of 4-6: 2-3 coding, 1 system design (senior+), 1 behavioral, sometimes domain deep dive (GPU/HPC) or project deep dive; then hiring committee/debrief and team match.
Senior: owns ambiguous multi-quarter problems end to end, sets technical direction, influences beyond the team, anticipates failure modes, mentors, and makes trade-offs explicit with data.

Get competing offers, negotiate total compensation (base, equity, sign-on, level), ask for the level and band, do not give the first number if avoidable, be polite and specific, get everything in writing.

column1: rocprof-compute vs rocprofv3 in one sentence?
column2: rocprofv3 collects raw traces and named counters; rocprof-compute is the analysis layer on top that schedules the counters a full analysis needs across passes, runs roofline benchmarks, and turns per-dispatch data into architecture-aware metrics and percent-of-peak (Nsight Compute over CUPTI analog).

column1: Why split rocprof-compute into profile and analyze modes?
column2: Profiling needs the GPU, ROCm, and the app; analysis needs only data, so it runs anywhere, repeatedly and cheaply, and can compare workloads; the workload directory is the contract between them.

column1: Most important data structure in rocprof-compute?
column2: The per-dispatch counter table: one row per dispatch (ID, kernel name, GPU, grid/workgroup size, LDS/VGPR/SGPR, timestamps), one column per counter. Metrics are vectorized expressions over the columns; passes join on dispatch identity, so that join key must be stable across replays.

column1: Why did rocprof-compute ratio metrics switch to SUM(A)/SUM(B)?
column2: AVG of per-dispatch ratios weights a tiny kernel equally with a huge one (e.g. 90% and 10% hit rates average to 50% though traffic-weighted it is 10%). The ratio of totals weights each dispatch by its denominator. Changed in 3.7.0.

column1: User says profiling takes 40 minutes. What do you do?
column2: Measure: app runtime x number of passes + roofline time. Reduce: filter kernels (-k) and dispatches, restrict blocks/sets to the metrics needed, shorten the app (fewer iterations), skip roofline if not needed, use multiplexing/single-pass sets where supported.

On architectures that can co-issue VALU instructions, active-instruction cycles can exceed the single-issue budget assumed by the denominator. The counter is fine; the peak definition assumes single issue.

Single file, no server, readable from any language, queryable with SQL (top kernels by L2 miss rate), supports versioned schemas. Weak for huge columnar analytics (Parquet is better) and concurrent writers, which do not matter for a post-processing artifact.

column1: Why is a metric N/A or empty, and is it a bug?
column2: Often not: the counter was not collected (filtered blocks/sets), the counter does not exist on that arch, the denominator is zero (kernel did no such accesses), or the metric is unsupported in that mode. Check collected counters and arch config first.

column1: Why declarative YAML metric configs plus an expression engine?
column2: Metrics are data, versioned per architecture, reviewable by hardware experts, and evaluated safely (parse and allow-list expressions, no arbitrary code) over the counter table; adding a metric needs no Python change. Downside: a mini-language to maintain and debug.
Each value has one owner; when the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped (RAII); ownership moves on assignment for non-Copy types (no implicit deep copies).

At any time either one mutable reference (&mut T) or any number of shared references (&T), and references must not outlive the value. Enforced at compile time by the borrow checker, which rules out data races in safe code.
Annotations ('a) that tell the compiler how long references are valid relative to each other so it can reject dangling references; mostly elided by rules. They do not change run-time behavior.

Send: safe to transfer ownership to another thread. Sync: safe to share &T between threads (T is Sync iff &T is Send). Rc is neither; Arc<T> is Send+Sync if T is Send+Sync; RefCell is Send but not Sync; Mutex<T> makes T shareable.

column1: Rust Box, Rc, Arc, RefCell vs C++?
column2: Box<T> ~ unique_ptr. Rc<T> ~ non-atomic shared_ptr (single thread). Arc<T> ~ shared_ptr with atomic count. RefCell<T>: runtime-checked borrowing (panics on violation). Weak<T> ~ weak_ptr.
Result<T, E> and Option<T> with the ? operator to propagate, like std::expected; panics for unrecoverable bugs (unwind or abort). No exceptions.

column1: Rust traits vs C++ concepts/virtual functions?
column2: Traits define shared behavior; generics with trait bounds are monomorphized (static dispatch like templates with concepts); dyn Trait uses a fat pointer (data + vtable) for dynamic dispatch.

column1: What does unsafe allow in Rust?
column2: Dereferencing raw pointers, calling unsafe functions/FFI, accessing mutable statics, implementing unsafe traits, accessing union fields. It does not turn off the borrow checker for references; you promise the invariants.

Goroutines are user-space tasks with small growable stacks (2 KiB initially), multiplexed M:N onto OS threads by the Go scheduler (G-M-P model); cheap to create millions. Blocking syscalls hand off the P so other goroutines continue.

Unbuffered: send blocks until a receiver takes it (synchronization point). Buffered: send blocks only when full. Close signals no more values; receiving from closed returns zero value and ok=false; sending on closed panics.

column1: Go select and common concurrency bugs?
column2: select waits on multiple channel ops (default makes it non-blocking). Bugs: goroutine leaks blocked on channels nobody reads, data races on maps (use sync.Mutex or channels; run with -race), loop-variable capture (fixed in Go 1.22).

Implicit (structural) satisfaction: a type implements an interface by having the methods, no declaration. Interface values are (type, value) pairs; a nil pointer inside a non-nil interface is not == nil.

Concurrent tri-color mark-and-sweep, non-moving, non-generational, tuned for low pause times (sub-millisecond typical); GOGC controls heap growth vs CPU trade-off, GOMEMLIMIT sets a soft memory limit.
Propagates cancellation, deadlines, and request-scoped values across API boundaries and goroutines; functions take ctx as the first parameter and return when ctx.Done() closes.

Break circular wait: number the forks and always pick up the lower-numbered first (or one philosopher picks in reverse order), or use a waiter/semaphore allowing at most N-1 to sit. Use scoped_lock for both forks in C++.

column1: Print odd/even numbers alternately with two threads?
column2: Shared counter, mutex, and condition variable; each thread waits until (counter % 2) matches its parity, prints, increments, notify_all. Or two semaphores ping-ponging. Avoid busy-waiting.

Readers-preference (writers may starve), writers-preference (readers may starve), fair (FIFO via a turnstile mutex). std::shared_mutex provides a reader-writer lock with implementation-defined fairness.

column1: Producer-consumer with a bounded buffer: classic solution?
column2: Mutex plus not_full and not_empty condition variables (or two counting semaphores: empty slots and full slots plus a mutex). Always wait with a predicate loop.

Mutex, condition variable, count. count_down: lock, decrement, if 0 notify_all. wait: lock, cv.wait(lk, [&]{ return count == 0; }). C++20 has std::latch (single use) and std::barrier (reusable with a completion function).

Track a generation number: last arriving thread resets the count, increments generation, notify_all; others wait until generation changes. Without the generation, fast threads re-entering can be confused with the previous phase.

Min-heap of (run_time, task) protected by a mutex; a worker waits on a condition variable with wait_until(top run_time), re-checks on notify when an earlier task is inserted, runs due tasks outside the lock.
Lock striping (N mutexes over bucket ranges), per-bucket locks, read-copy-update, or lock-free open addressing. Resizing is the hard part (lock all stripes or incremental migration).
